node.label: Robert Alexander Innes
node.date_label: Oral history methods 1999–2000 · insider/outsider 2009 · Elder Brother and the Law of the People 2013 · 'Historians and Indigenous Genocide in Saskatchewan' and 'Clearing the Plains of Accountability' 2018 · open letter 2021
node.description: Historian of Cowessess First Nation, kinship and treaty land, and a critic of how historians have written the 1880s starvation policy. In 2018 he wrote that neither historians nor the Canadian government had acknowledged the starvation deaths of the early 1880s in Treaty 4 territory as genocide, and that historians who agreed the policy killed many had not tried to count the dead. Cowessess First Nation's own treaty land entitlement research had done that work. Historical records, he argued, do not tell a story by themselves, and decolonizing history can simply mean asking the right questions and looking in the right places. Against Daschuk's Clearing the Plains (2013), he held that Edgar Dewdney bore responsibility and that Daschuk misrepresented Tobias, Lux and Titley, whom he cites. Earlier he wrote on oral history methods in Native Studies and on insider research; he conceived Shekon Neechie (2018).
node.representative_figures_and_works: Robert Alexander Innes; 'Oral History Methods in Native Studies' (Oral History Forum, 1999–2000); 'Wait a Second. Who Are You Anyways?' (AIQ, 2009); Elder Brother and the Law of the People: Contemporary Kinship and Cowessess First Nation (UMP, 2013); 'Historians and Indigenous Genocide in Saskatchewan' and 'Clearing the Plains of Accountability' (Shekon Neechie, 2018). University of Saskatchewan (Indigenous Studies); McMaster University (2021).
node.scope_note: Read in full: the two Shekon Neechie essays of 21 June 2018 (the first also reposted on Active History, 12 June 2019; that page returned 403); USask News on Shekon Neechie (2018); the 2021 open letter. Known through publisher pages, a database excerpt or a citing reader: Elder Brother (2013), the 1999–2000 Oral History Forum article, the 2009 AIQ article. The essays' critique is his own; Daschuk's book, Tobias (1983), Lux (2004), Titley (1999) and Woolford's review are known here only as he quotes them. n. 5 of the 2018 essay records that the Canadian Historical Review declined it unless refocused 'away from a critique of historians'. History PhD citation graph, release 2026-10-23: cited by 27 Canadian History PhDs; context only.

proposed_edges.relationship: Daschuk's Clearing the Plains exonerates Edgar Dewdney by misrepresenting the historians it cites, and its praise suggests few readers checked the foundational literature (2018).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Paraphrased (Shekon Neechie, community-controlled: cited, not reproduced). 'Clearing the Plains of Accountability' (2018), para. 2 (his aim: to hold Daschuk's argument against the scholars he cites); paras. 5–8 (Tobias 1983, Lux 2004 and Titley 1999 set against Daschuk on Dewdney); para. 14 (whether those who praised the book read the foundational literature). 'Historians and Indigenous Genocide in Saskatchewan', para. 15 (Daschuk's attempt to exonerate Dewdney contradicts previous historians). Daschuk's words are known only through Innes. Ends in Agent B's field (strand health_starvation); B to confirm.

proposed_edges.relationship: Historians of the 1880s starvation policy agreed it killed many yet none called it genocide or tried to count the dead; records do not tell a story by themselves (2018).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Paraphrased (Shekon Neechie: cited, not reproduced). 'Historians and Indigenous Genocide in Saskatchewan' (2018), para. 2 (neither historians nor the government acknowledged genocide in Treaty 4 territory; why none counted the deaths); para. 13 (Tobias, Lux, Daschuk and Titley avoid the term); para. 16 (against Woolford's defence of Daschuk: records do not speak for themselves); para. 17 (why historians did not look for the evidence). Fairness: he builds on Tobias and Lux ('Clearing the Plains of Accountability', paras. 5–6). Ends in Agent A's field; A to confirm.

proposed_edges.relationship: Points to Cowessess First Nation's own treaty land entitlement research as the count of the starvation policy's dead that historians never made: history asking the right questions and looking in the right places (2018).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Paraphrased (Shekon Neechie: cited, not reproduced; the community's figures are not reproduced, OCAP limits). 'Historians and Indigenous Genocide in Saskatchewan' (2018), paras. 21–25 (the band's treaty-land researchers traced members missing from annuity lists, work historians had not done); para. 29 (decolonizing history as asking the right questions and looking in the right places). USask News 2018: Innes conceived Shekon Neechie.
